theorems_and_key_concepts: Cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms, discovered by Robert Hooke in 1665.
Unicellular organisms (Amoeba, Paramecium) vs Multicellular organisms.
Levels of structural organisation: Cells -> Tissues -> Organs -> Organ systems -> Organism.
Parts of a cell: Cell membrane (plasma membrane), Cytoplasm, and Nucleus.
Prokaryotic cells (bacteria, blue-green algae lacking nuclear membrane) vs Eukaryotic cells.
Organelles: Mitochondria (powerhouse of cell), Plastids (chloroplasts containing chlorophyll), Vacuoles.
Differences between plant and animal cells: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall, large central vacuole, and plastids.
learning_outcomes: Prepare temporary mounts of onion peel and human cheek cells.
Compare plant and animal cells using labelled diagrams.
Differentiate between prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms.

activities.title: Observation of Onion Peel Cells Under Compound Microscope
activities.aim: To prepare a temporary mount of onion peel cells and observe plant cell structures under a microscope.
procedure: Peel off a thin transparent epidermal layer from the fleshy scale of an onion using forceps.
Place the peel immediately in a watch glass containing water to prevent drying.
Transfer the peel onto a clean glass slide and add a drop of Safranin stain.
After 2 minutes, wash off excess stain with water and place a drop of glycerine.
Gently lower a cover slip using a needle avoiding air bubbles, and observe under low and high power of microscope.
precautions: The peel must not fold upon itself on the slide.
Avoid air bubbles beneath the cover slip by lowering it slowly with a needle.
activities.observations: Large numbers of brick-shaped rectangular cells are observed with distinct dark-stained cell walls, peripheral cytoplasm, prominent round nucleus, and large central vacuole.
activities.conclusion: Plant cells possess a definite cell wall, cytoplasm, and nucleus, demonstrating that cell is the structural unit of plants.

activities.title: Observation of Human Cheek Cells
activities.aim: To prepare a temporary stained mount of human cheek epithelial cells to observe animal cell structure.
procedure: Gently scrape the inner lining of your cheek with the blunt end of a clean toothpick.
Spread the scraped material onto a drop of water on a clean glass slide.
Add a drop of methylene blue stain and let it stand for one minute.
Cover with a cover slip and examine under the microscope.
precautions: Scrape very gently without hurting the cheek epithelium.
Always use a fresh, sterile toothpick.
activities.observations: Irregular polygonal cells are seen scattered on the slide. Each cell has a thin cell membrane, granular cytoplasm, and a centrally located dark nucleus. No cell wall is present.
activities.conclusion: Animal cells lack a cell wall and chloroplasts, possessing only a flexible plasma membrane around the cytoplasm.

theorems_and_key_concepts: Microorganisms are microscopic living creatures classified into Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa, and Algae.
Viruses are microscopic entities that reproduce only inside the host cells of plants, animals, or bacteria.
Friendly microorganisms: Making of curd and bread (Lactobacillus, Yeast fermentation), Commercial production of alcohol and acetic acid.
Medicinal use of microorganisms: Antibiotics (Alexander Fleming, Penicillin 1929), Vaccines (Edward Jenner, Smallpox vaccine 1798).
Increasing soil fertility: Nitrogen fixing bacteria (Rhizobium, Blue-green algae).
Harmful microorganisms: Pathogens causing communicable diseases (Cholera, Tuberculosis, Typhoid, Malaria, Dengue).
Food poisoning and Food preservation methods: Chemical methods, Common salt, Sugar, Oil and vinegar, Heat and cold treatments (Pasteurization - Louis Pasteur), Storage and packing.
Nitrogen cycle: Nitrogen fixation, ammonification, nitrification, and denitrification.
learning_outcomes: Classify microorganisms into major groups.
Explain the role of yeast in baking and alcohol fermentation.
Describe methods of food preservation and illustrate the Nitrogen cycle.

activities.title: Observing Fermentation by Yeast
activities.aim: To demonstrate that yeast produces carbon dioxide gas during the fermentation of sugar.
procedure: Take 100 mL of warm water in a conical flask, add two teaspoons of sugar and half a teaspoon of baker's yeast.
Stir well and stretch the neck of a deflated rubber balloon over the mouth of the flask.
Keep the flask in a warm place for 3 to 4 hours and observe the balloon.
precautions: Water must be warm, not hot, to prevent killing the yeast cells.
Ensure the balloon fits tightly over the flask neck.
activities.observations: The balloon gradually inflates and stands erect due to gas accumulation. A pleasant fruity alcohol smell is emitted from the flask.
activities.conclusion: Yeast reproduces rapidly and breaks down sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide gas (fermentation), which inflates the balloon.

theorems_and_key_concepts: Crops: When plants of the same kind are cultivated at one place on a large scale. Kharif crops (sown in rainy season: Paddy, Maize, Soyabean) and Rabi crops (sown in winter: Wheat, Gram, Mustard).

Basic agricultural practices: Preparation of soil (ploughing, levelling), Sowing (good quality seeds, seed drill), Adding manure and fertilisers, Irrigation, Protecting from weeds, Harvesting, and Storage.
Differences between organic manure and chemical fertilisers (NPK).
Modern irrigation systems: Sprinkler system (uneven sandy soil) and Drip system (delivers water drop by drop directly to roots, zero water wastage).
Weed management: Physical weeding, Weedicides (2,4-D).
Harvesting, Threshing, and Storage: Granaries, Silos, buffer stock by Food Corporation of India (FCI).
learning_outcomes: Distinguish between Kharif and Rabi cropping seasons.
Compare traditional and modern irrigation methods (Drip and Sprinkler).
Explain advantages of organic manure over chemical fertilisers.

activities.title: Separating Healthy Seeds from Damaged Seeds
activities.aim: To separate viable healthy seeds from hollow damaged ones using the flotation method.
apparatus: A handful of gram or wheat seeds
procedure: Fill half of the beaker with clean water.
Put a handful of wheat seeds into the beaker and stir thoroughly with a glass rod.
Allow the mixture to settle undisturbed for 5 minutes and observe.
precautions: Stir gently to dislodge any air bubbles clinging to the seeds.
Let the water come to complete rest before observation.
activities.observations: A few damaged, hollow, insect-eaten seeds float on the surface of the water, whereas healthy, dense, undamaged seeds sink to the bottom.
activities.conclusion: Healthy seeds are heavier and sink, providing a simple household technique for selecting viable seeds for sowing.

theorems_and_key_concepts: Reproduction is essential for the continuation of a species.
Modes of reproduction: Sexual reproduction (fusion of male and female gametes) and Asexual reproduction (single parent).
Male reproductive system: Testes (produce sperms and testosterone), Sperm ducts, and Penis. Structure of human sperm.
Female reproductive system: Ovaries (produce ova/eggs and estrogen), Oviducts (Fallopian tubes), and Uterus.
Fertilisation: Fusion of sperm nucleus with egg nucleus to form a zygote. Internal fertilisation (humans, cows, birds) vs External fertilisation (frogs, fish).
In vitro fertilisation (IVF) and test-tube babies.
Development of embryo: Zygote divides repeatedly into an embryo, implants in the uterine wall, and develops into a fetus.
Viviparous animals (give birth to young ones) vs Oviparous animals (lay eggs).
Metamorphosis in frog: Egg -> Tadpole (larva) -> Adult frog.
Asexual reproduction in animals: Budding in Hydra and Binary fission in Amoeba.
learning_outcomes: Identify male and female reproductive organs in humans.
Differentiate between internal and external fertilisation.
Explain budding in Hydra and binary fission in Amoeba.

activities.title: Observation of Binary Fission in Amoeba and Budding in Hydra
activities.aim: To observe permanent slides showing asexual reproduction in Amoeba (binary fission) and Hydra (budding).
apparatus: Permanent slides of binary fission in Amoeba
Permanent slides of budding in Hydra
procedure: Place the slide of binary fission in Amoeba on the microscope stage.
Focus under low power and then switch to high power; observe nucleus division and constriction in cytoplasm.
Replace with the slide of budding in Hydra and observe the tiny outgrowth (bud) arising from the parent body.
precautions: Handle permanent slides carefully to avoid scratching the coverslip.
Use fine adjustment for sharp cellular focusing.
activities.observations: In Amoeba, the nucleus elongates and divides into two, followed by cytoplasmic cleavage into two daughter cells. In Hydra, a bulb-like bud develops tentacles and detaches from the parent.
activities.conclusion: Amoeba reproduces asexually by binary fission, whereas Hydra reproduces asexually by budding.

theorems_and_key_concepts: Adolescence is the period of life between 11 and 19 years when body undergoes changes leading to reproductive maturity.
Puberty: Onset of sexual maturity marked by sudden increase in height, changes in body shape, voice change (Adam's apple in boys).
Development of sex organs and secondary sexual characteristics (facial hair in boys, breast development in girls).
Role of hormones: Endocrine glands release hormones directly into the bloodstream to reach target sites.
Pituitary gland (master gland), Thyroid (thyroxine), Pancreas (insulin), Adrenal glands (adrenaline - fight or flight).
Sex hormones: Testosterone in males, Estrogen in females.
Menstrual cycle in females: Menarche (first menstruation) and Menopause (stoppage around 45-50 years).
Sex determination in human baby: Father determines the sex (X sperm -> girl child XX; Y sperm -> boy child XY).
Nutritional needs of adolescents, personal hygiene, and saying NO to drugs.
learning_outcomes: Describe physical and emotional changes occurring during puberty.
Explain the genetic mechanism of sex determination in humans.
Understand the importance of balanced diet and hygiene during adolescence.
key_formulas_and_equations: \text{Height calculation} = \frac{\text{Present height (cm)}}{\%\text{ of full height at this age}} \times 100

activities.title: Estimating Predicted Full Adult Height Based on Growth Charts
activities.aim: To calculate the predicted adult height of an adolescent using standardized SCERT age-growth percentage data.
apparatus: Growth rate percentage table for boys and girls
procedure: Measure the exact present height of a 13-year-old student standing straight against a wall.
Consult the growth chart table (e.g. boys at 13 have reached approximately 92% of adult height; girls 95%).
Apply the formula: Predicted Height = (Present height / % from table) * 100.
precautions: Student must stand barefoot with heels, back, and head touching the vertical wall.
Ensure the measuring scale is horizontal.
activities.observations: For a 13-year-old boy of 138 cm height, predicted adult height = (138 / 92) * 100 = 150 cm.
activities.conclusion: Growth spurts during adolescence follow standard physiological trends regulated by growth hormones.

theorems_and_key_concepts: Deforestation and its consequences: Loss of habitat, desertification, global warming, disrupted water cycle, soil erosion.
Droughts and floods caused by destruction of vegetative catchment areas.
Biodiversity: Variety of plants, animals, and microorganisms existing in an area.
Protected areas: Wildlife Sanctuaries (protection to wild animals), National Parks (preservation of flora, fauna, and landscape), Biosphere Reserves (multipurpose protected zones like Pachmarhi).
Flora (plants of an area) and Fauna (animals of an area).
Endemic species: Species found exclusively in a particular geographical area.
Endangered species and Red Data Book published by IUCN.
Migration of birds (Siberian cranes travelling thousands of miles to avoid severe winter).
Recycling of paper (saves 17 full-grown trees per tonne of paper) and Reforestation.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the consequences of deforestation on rainfall and soil fertility.
Differentiate between a Wildlife Sanctuary and a National Park.
Promote reforestation and paper recycling in daily life.
key_formulas_and_equations: 1\text{ Tonne of Recycled Paper} = \text{Saves } 17\text{ Mature Trees} + 26{,}000\text{ Litres Water}

activities.title: Surveying Endemic and Endangered Species of Andhra Pradesh
activities.aim: To identify endemic and endangered flora and fauna of Andhra Pradesh using secondary data.
apparatus: Reference books and forest survey reports
procedure: Gather information about protected wildlife reserves in Andhra Pradesh (e.g. Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary, Rollapadu Wildlife Sanctuary, Sri Venkateswara National Park).
List prominent endangered animals such as Great Indian Bustard, Olive Ridley Sea Turtle, and Red Sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus).
Classify them into endemic, endangered, and vulnerable categories.
precautions: Verify scientific names and conservation status from authoritative forest sources.
activities.observations: Rollapadu sanctuary is the prime grassland habitat for the critically endangered Great Indian Bustard in Kurnool district; Red Sanders is endemic to the Seshachalam hills.
activities.conclusion: Habitat conservation and dedicated wildlife sanctuaries are indispensable to prevent extinction of endemic and endangered species.

theorems_and_key_concepts: Air pollution: Contamination of air by unwanted substances harmful to living organisms and non-living things.
Air pollutants: Carbon monoxide (incomplete combustion), Carbon dioxide, Sulphur dioxide and Nitrogen oxides (cause acid rain), Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs deplete ozone layer), Smog (smoke + fog).
Case study: Taj Mahal yellowing due to acid rain from Mathura refinery ('Marble Cancer').
Greenhouse effect and Global Warming: Carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide trapping heat.
Water pollution: Contamination of water bodies by industrial effluents, untreated sewage, agricultural pesticides, and fertilizers.
Case study: River Ganga pollution and Namami Gange programme.
Eutrophication: Excessive algae growth depleting dissolved oxygen in water, suffocating aquatic life.
Potable water: Water that is safe for drinking. Purification methods: Filtration, Boiling, Chlorination.
learning_outcomes: Identify primary causes and consequences of air and water pollution.
Explain the phenomenon of acid rain and its impact on monuments and soil.
Describe methods to obtain potable water at household and community levels.

activities.title: Testing Water Quality and Suspended Impurities
activities.aim: To compare physical parameters (turbidity, odour, pH) of tap water, pond water, and drain water.
apparatus: Water samples (Tap water, Stagnant pond water, Drain water)
procedure: Collect 100 mL each of tap water, pond water, and drain water in three labeled beakers.
Observe the colour, clarity, and smell of each sample.
Filter equal volumes through filter paper and check for suspended residue.
Dip a strip of pH paper into each sample and compare with the standard pH colour chart.
precautions: Do not taste any water sample.
Wash hands thoroughly with soap after handling drain and pond water.
activities.observations: Tap water is clear, odourless, with neutral pH (approx 7.0). Pond water is slightly turbid with microscopic algae and greenish residue. Drain water is dark, foul-smelling, and acidic.
activities.conclusion: Surface and wastewater contain physical and chemical contaminants that require multi-stage treatment before being safe for human consumption.
